subtopic: MR. MACQUARRIE-INFORMATION GIVEN TO PRESS BY MINISTER BEFORE DISCLOSURE TO PARLIAMENT
MR. MACQUARRIE-INFORMATION GIVEN TO PRESS BY MINISTER BEFORE DISCLOSURE TO PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning the failure of the Postmaster General to table in this house the report of the consulting firm of Kates Peat Marwick and Company which was commissioned to study the workings of his department, and especially his action in discussing this matter with a reporter before making it available to members of this house.
In this morning's Financial Post the following appears:
Communications Minister Eric Kierans is scheduled to table a remarkable document next week in the Commons.
There follows a commentary, and evidently an interpretation of this document by the minister. This growing tendency of members of the ministry to communicate to persons and groups outside this house information which should be properly conveyed to hon. members amounts to an erosion of the respect properly due from the executive to the people's representatives.
That this is not the first failure of the Postmaster General to give parliament information available to him is indicated by the fact that an earlier report of the same consulting firm was presented to the minister on November 19, 1968 and has not yet been tabled in the house or made available to members. On general principle I protest that such practices by ministers breach the privileges of parliament.
Any blockage in the flow of information to parliament in reference to the Post Office, a department about which there is currently such widespread and justifiable criticism and dissatisfaction among the Canadian public, is particularly reprehensible and indeed inexcusable.

subtopic: RELEASE TO ARCHIVES OF RECORDS IN EXISTENCE FOR THIRTY YEARS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: RELEASE TO ARCHIVES OF RECORDS IN EXISTENCE FOR THIRTY YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce a policy to make available for research and other public use as large a portion of the records of the Canadian government prior to July 1, 1939 as would be consistent with the national interest. The cabinet secretariat and the departments and agencies of government are being asked to transfer to the Public Archives
May 1. 1969
8200	COMMONS
Release of Old Documents to Archives official records which are more than 30 years old to be made available to the public under the normal rules of access in force in the Public Archives.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)

Certain records will be exempted from public access, particularly those the release of which might adversely affect Canada's external relations, violate the right of privacy of individuals, or adversely affect the national security. However, it is the intention that a vast portion of Canada's records prior to mid-1939 will be transferred to the Public Archives during the current year, and that annual transfers be made in subsequent years.
While certain of the records to be made available to the public have already been transferred to the Public Archives, the majority are still in the hands of the cabinet secretariat and the various departments and agencies of government. The volume of files is such that it will take some time to screen and arrange for an orderly flow of documents to the Archives. Within these practical limitations, however, every effort will be made to provide public access to these papers as promptly as possible, beginning on July 1, 1969.
The general rule will be that, with the exceptions noted, all records over 30 years old will be transferred to the Archives and made available to the public. In addition, departments and agencies will be encouraged to transfer to the Archives records less than 30 years old, in so far as this would be consistent with the efficient operation of the departments or agencies involved. Although these more recent records would remain under the control of the minister concerned, they could be made available to the public under terms and conditions to be established by the responsible minister in consultation with the Dominion Archivist. As for records less than 30 years old and which are retained in the custody of departments and agencies, controlled access may be permitted in special cases, again under terms and conditions to be established by the minister in consultation with the Dominion Archivist.

Because of the nature of cabinet and cabinet committee documents and minutes, they will in no case be made available for public examination until they are 30 years old. Former Prime Ministers and ministers will,


of course, be given access on request to such of those records as originated during their various periods of office, in order to refresh their memories.
Of particular interest in future years, beginning in 1970, will be the release of annual portions of records of the cabinet war committee for the period 1940 to 1945. In 1974, records of the deliberations of the cabinet will begin to be made available, the first formal recording of its proceedings having begun in early 1944.
In announcing this policy I should like to express the government's belief that it will meet with the approval of Canadian scholars, members of learned societies and others interested in the history of Canadian government. In a broader sense, it exemplifies the government's desire to stimulate interest and participation in the affairs of government by Canadians generally.

subsubtopic: U.S. PRESS RELEASE ON CANADIAN RECOGNITION OF MAINLAND CHINA-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ABOUT NIGERIA-BIAFRA HOSTILITIES-UNITED NATIONS INVOLVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for two purposes. The first is to table an exchange which took place at a press briefing given by the United States State Department spokesman on February 11, 1969, relating to the Canadian government's announcement of its intention to negotiate with the representatives of Peking for an exchange of diplomats; the second is to make a brief report, as requested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), on the representations made by our ambassador in Lagos to the Nigerian government.
Representations Mr. Malone made included a reiteration of our concern at the reports of bombings of non-military targets in the rebel area, the question of a cease fire and ways of improving relief deliveries. General Gowon shared our concern at the reports of bombings of civilians and reaffirmed that strict orders had been given to avoid, where possible, civilian casualties. I am pleased to note that there has been a notable absence of reports of bombings for some time. As to a cease fire, it was confirmed that the situation with regard to a cease fire and a negotiated settlement remained unchanged. As I have told the house on many occasions, until conditions and terms exist which are acceptable to both disputants, prospects for an early cessation of hostilities will remain remote. With regard to relief, the High Commissioner reiterated the government's support for efforts to conclude agreed arrangements for relief deliveries by day into the Uli and Obilago airstrips.
I was also asked by the Leader of the Opposition about possible United Nations involvement. In that regard I believe it would be useful for the house to have the following excerpt from a press conference given by the Secretary-General of the United Nations on April 17 of this year. I quote:
-the United Nations cannot be involved in a crisis situation which is declared by the member state concerned to be an internal matter under Article 2 (7). This point of view is endorsed and supported by the whole Organization of African Unity. So, in the face of this attitude by the Organization of African Unity, I do not believe that any member of the United Nations has any desire to inscribe the item, "The Situation in Nigeria", before a principal organ of the United Nations.
External Affairs
If I may anticipate something, if any member state were to bring this item, "The Situation in Nigeria", before the Security Council or the United Nations General Assembly, I am sure that the item would not be inscribed on the agenda. So it does not make any difference whether any member state tries to inscribe this on the agenda or the Secretary General tries to inscribe it on the agenda. From a realistic point of view, any such attempt would not succeed because of the knowledge that the Organization of African Unity is against such a course as the inscription of an item on the agenda of either the Security Council or the United Nations General Assembly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the information he has given to the house about suggestions made on behalf of the government of Canada to the government of Nigeria and for the statement he made about the United Nations. I cannot help feeling that here we have a most unsatisfactory state of affairs. As a member of the Commonwealth and of a group of civilized nations, it seems to me that Canada has a greater responsibility towards those suffering and dying in Nigeria than has so far been discharged. It is estimated that more than a million people have died as a result of that war.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the government of this country should exercise its diligence in trying to organize, in consultation with other countries and particularly Commonwealth countries, an effort to terminate the war, bring about a ceasefire and a cessation of shipments of arms. They should make a real effort to terminate the suffering and dying that is going on in that country.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
I am not minimizing the difficulties which exist, Mr. Speaker. I suggest in all seriousness that what is happening in Nigeria, the number who are dying as a direct result of the war is a very sad commentary indeed on the civilized nations of this world, of which this country has been proud to be part, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that his statement is totally unsatisfactory to those who are really concerned with seeking a solution to the problem in Nigeria and Biafra and seeking some alleviation of the terrible suffering by the people in Biafra.
First I wish to say to him, Mr. Speaker, that while I have the greatest respect for the Secretary General of the United Nations, his

Inquiry into Non-Medical uses of Drugs word is not yet the last word on everything concerning that organization. Indeed I remind the Secretary of State for External Affairs that just about two years ago the Secretary General of the United Nations made a certain decision with regard to UNEF in the Middle East. Both the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs at that time did not hesitate to criticize that decision and action.
I am not satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that because the Secretary General of the United Nations, with his great experience and knowledge, says that something should be done a certain way, that this is the way it must be. I am not satisfied that it means that Canada or any other member of the United Nations! should not make some attempt to have this matter discussed in the international forum. They should search for a possible cessation of the terrible fighting in Nigeria.
I did not have a copy of the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but as I listened I noted the fact that the Secretary General of the United Nations spoke about the Security Council and the United Nations General Assembly. I remind the minister that my colleagues and myself have asked him many times to inscribe this subject, not on the agenda of the Security General or General Assembly, but on the agenda of the Third Committee of the United Nations which deals with humanitarian, cultural and other matters. In my humble opinion, this matter should be put on the agenda of the Third Committee and discussed. This would be the starting point for an international consideration of the problem.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, I am totally dissatisfied with the approach of our ambassador in Lagos. He has offered help under certain conditions. Canada is able to make assistance available now through various organizations for the building of the new airstrip which they are attempting to build in Biafra. There are also other ways to alleviate the suffering of those people.
I have said from time to time, and I now repeat the fact, that the civilized world has not reacted to the terrible fratricidal war in that country, the fact that a conflict like that can go on for two years-in two months it will be two years-with 1 million to 2 million people dying, mainly of hunger, and the civilized world keeps its hands off. All this reminds me of many instances in history where this kind of barbarity was permitted to go on, and everybody called non-intervention,

with the result that the barbarity ended in colossal difficulties for the world as a whole. One of the matters of which the government cannot be proud is the constant excuses for inaction that the government has given in the case of the terrible war in Nigeria.

subsubtopic: U.S. PRESS RELEASE ON CANADIAN RECOGNITION OF MAINLAND CHINA-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ABOUT NIGERIA-BIAFRA HOSTILITIES-UNITED NATIONS INVOLVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe everybody is deeply affected by what is happening in Nigeria.
However, everyone must at the same time recognize that the internal policy of that country is not the concern of Canada nor that of the United States.
Although some people protest because Canada does not go to Nigeria to re-establish peace and ask Nigeria to accept the Biafrans as they are, there are not many to protest, for example, against Russia invading Czechoslovakia and crushing those who want to be free.
Mr. Speaker, I say again that we would like to see an end to the Nigerian war. However, it does not come to an end and the only thing Canada can do, in my opinion, is to put before the United Nations an agreement proposal between the Biafrans and the Nigerian people. Their domestic policy is their own business.
In fact, we would not accept that these people interfere in ours. We are ourselves involved in domestic feuds, without bloodshed yet, but what assurance do we have that we will not be facing such situations in the future.
I say again that these countries' domestic policy is their own business, and that Canada, as a so-called peaceful nation, can encourage them to settle their differences and advise them, but it not desirable to interfere directly in their domestic policy, because that is no concern of ours.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING COMMITTEE INQUIRY INTO NON-MEDICAL USES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the government plans to establish a committee of inquiry to examine into and make recommendations respecting the non-medical use of drugs and related substances in Canada.
The establishment of this committee of inquiry reflects the grave concern felt by the government at the expanding proportions of
May 1, 1969

the use of drugs and related substances for non-medical purposes. This committee will consist of five members and be directed to pursue the following objects:	(a) to marshal from available sources, both in Canada and abroad, data and information comprising the present fund of knowledge concerning the non-medical use of sedative, stimulant, tran-quilizing, hallucinogenic and other psychotropic drugs or substances;
(b)	to report on the current state of medical knowledge respecting the effect of the drugs and substances referred to in (a);
(c)	to inquire into and report on the motivation underlying the non-medical use referred to in (a);
(d)	to inquire into and report on the social, economic, educational and philosophical factors relating to the use for non-medical purposes of the drugs and substances referred to in (a) and in particular on the extent of the phenomenon, the social factors that have led to it, the age groups involved, and problems of communication; and
(e)	to inquire into and recommend with respect to the ways or means by which the federal government can act, alone or in its relations with government at other levels, in the reduction of the dimensions of the problems involved in such use.
The committee will have the authority contained in Part 2 of the Inquiries Act and be assisted, as required, by officials of appropriate departments and agencies of government. It will be authorized to invite, receive and consider submissions from organizations and individuals.
It is anticipated that the committee will make an official report of its progress within six months of its establishment and periodically thereafter, with a final report to be presented within two years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of non-confidence before the house this afternoon was not drafted without a great deal of serious consideration of all of its implications. Certainly there is no conceivable op-

portunity to defeat the government with its numerical superiority in the house at this time. But if the motion serves to draw to Your Honour's attention and that of hon. members opposite the very serious plight of all segments of the agricultural industry today, it will have served its purpose.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I am supported in moving this motion, Mr. Speaker, by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam). The reason I asked for his support, which was granted quite eagerly, was to emphasize that this problem exists in all parts of Canada, from the east coast to the west coast. It is a problem on which public attention has been focused because of the dire position of the wheat growers and grain growers of western Canada and of the farmers of eastern Canada, but the economic problem is not confined to them.
I was rather alarmed, indeed shocked, to learn when travelling in the west that a minister or ministers of the Crown in meeting with farmers there had implied that one of the reasons no solutions were being put forward by the government to alleviate the farmers' economic problems was that they could not obtain the understanding, the consideration or the sympathy of eastern Canada. I reject that theory in its entirety. It is the old one of divide and conquer. We in eastern Canada are very much aware of the problems in the west. The only major difference is that many farmers in the west are unable to dispose of their crops while farmers in eastern Canada, although they can sell their crops, in many instances must sell them below the cost of production. Therefore Canadian farmers in general are directly concerned with the government's agricultural policy, and they have every right to be concerned because it directly affects their livelihood.
Many grave criticisms have been expressed by leaders of agricultural groups about the lack of policy of the government, about the confused policies of the government, about agricultural policies that seem to be working toward opposite ends. Surely after almost seven years in office the government should be able to indicate to the great agricultural industry where it thinks its place should be in our economic life, what its long-term and short-term goals should be, and what the future is for the young Canadian farmer. These are questions that should be answered.
May 1, 1969

But whenever questions have been asked in the house over the last few months by members of opposition parties we have heard the old refrain that agriculture has never had it so good, that production has increased, that many new products are being produced, that the gross national income is higher than it has ever been, that inventories on farms are at their highest in history. And then there was the ridiculous observation by a former minister of agriculture when he attempted to indicate how good things were for Canadian farmers by saying that never before had the farmers of this nation borrowed so much money.
In answering these allegations I draw the attention of hon. members opposite to the steady parade of farmers to the banks and other lending institutions, seeking money not only to run their operations but to live on and to clothe and educate their families. I draw the attention of hon. members opposite to the growing total of accounts receivable held by business firms dealing with farmers. I draw their attention to the rural and weekly newspapers where they will find page after page after page of paid announcements of sales of farm machinery and livestock by countless farmers who have simply said, "We have had enough and we must get out." I draw their attention to the drop in sales experienced by businesses connected with farming, to the drop in sales of fertilizer in certain areas, to the drop in sales of new farm machinery, new farm equipment, chemicals and all the other things that are normal to the agricultural business. Surely the farmers of this nation deserve an indication from the government either that they are no longer considered a viable part of the Canadian economy or that the government will take its full responsibility toward them by saying, "We feel you are indispensable; we will take the responsibility of providing an economic climate for you that will enable you to derive from your capital investment and labour a return comparable with that received by all other segments of the economy."
To indicate the tremendous confusion in the government's approach to agriculture I shall deal with a few specific commodities. I shall not deal with wheat and feed grains because some of my colleagues and members of other parties no doubt will do so. As an example, look at the dairy industry. Here is an industry in which there is a tremendous investment. By its very nature it must be considered in the context of a long-term economic plan, but
Business of Supply
within the last five years we have had five separate and distinct government policies for that industry.
We have a National Dairy Commission whose sole purpose seems to be to curtail Canadian production so that it will just meet the demands of our domestic market. But when we travel across the country we see thousands of pounds of imported butter simply because some sections of the country are unable to provide for their own needs. A quota system was set up that was supposed to put farmers on an equal basis from coast to coast. But quotas totalling millions of pounds have now been transferred from the west, an area that does not produce all its own dairy requirements, to eastern Canada where we normally produce more than we consume. This does not seem justifiable, practical or reasonable. In addition, the way subsidies are being implemented means that many small dairy businesses are being forced out of business, and it is becoming financially impossible for a young farmer to enter that business.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
What about the greenhouse industry? We had a pronouncement by the minister that this industry was in difficulty and that people should be encouraged to leave it. We are not dealing with just hundreds of thousands of dollars in this industry. We are dealing with an industry in which millions of dollars are invested. This industry was based on government action. The fact that the government has not placed tariffs against the importation of specialized food has made it practically impossible economically for the industry to develop in a profitable way. In its desire to have cheaper food and bring down the cost of living the government is jeopardizing this entire industry.
What about the tobacco industry? Here we have a multi-million dollar industry which has brought untold wealth to the provinces in which this product is grown. We have the impossible situation of one government department spending thousands of dollars in experimental work in order to increase production and quality while another department of the government issues propaganda designed to stop the use of this product and curtail the industry. Here the government has a golden opportunity. By shifting its emphasis in research, surely to goodness it could provide methods by which, if there are dangerous components in tobacco, they could be removed to the benefit of the industry, the government and the people.

May 1. 1969
Business of Supply
What about the poultry industry? In Canada we have a poultry industry which is endeavouring by the organization of national commissions to regiment and control the marketing of its produce in an orderly fashion. This is being done at the request of the provincial and federal governments. We know right now that, unless the government proposes to change its policy, importations of poultry, eggs and other allied products will flood into this country from other nations and take up any slack in our market.
Let us look at the canning industry. We had a strong viable canning industry from coast to coast. We were proud of the quality of the pack and proud of the fact that the industry provided an income for hundreds of farmers and their families in almost every province of this nation. What has happened? The government has allowed the importation, especially of fruits and some vegetables, into this country to a degree that is forcing the industry right out of business. We are told that we must allow this because of our agreements and tariff commitments. The fact is that the government in every instance has failed to take any step to protect Canadian industry.
It is not good enough to make excuses. It is not good enough to procrastinate until the damage is done. It is not good enough to come into the house and say, "We cannot, because". I point out that every nation in the world today with excess products is selling them and a lot of this surplus is coming into Canada. Surely it is time we took our place among the trading nations of the world and traded on our terms and not just on their terms.
There was a task force hearing. Government policy was held up because we were to have a congress to which the task force would report. I have a great deal of admiration for the work the task force has done. I compliment those responsible for setting up the congress and for the manner in which the meetings where carried on. One thing that disturbs me, however, is the fact that the task force seemed to be directed wholly to the one proposition of getting the government completely out of agriculture and letting it stand on its own feet.
I have before me a book about the size of Eaton's or Simpsons-Sears fall and winter catalogue. It contains 385 pages devoted entirely to the government's involvement in agriculture. Now we see at all levels of government a move toward complete abandonment. We are now at cross-purposes. We

heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) get up in the house and announce a change in hog premiums. This was good; it was asked for by the industry. We were told it was designed to increase the quality of hogs in Canada. It was acceptable and reasonable. I take issue with it, however, because within 90 days the minister announced another policy which was not based on the report of the task force and was not announced after the congress met. It was not done in consultation with the industry. It was designed solely not to increase the efficiency of the hog producers but simply to save the government X million dollars for no other reason than that it wished to have nothing to do with the agricultural industry.
This brings me to the subject of tariffs. It has always been a source of amazement to me and to other hon. members that whenever a tariff question comes up and one of our industries finds itself in economic chaos the government merely says it is aware of the problem. We are told by members of the government that they have listened to the representations and are in sympathy with them but cannot do anything. They tell us there are agreements and that we must wait upon the Gatt threaty. We have to wait for its conclusion, we have to wait for its inception, we have to wait for its deliberations. We must wait. This is not good enough.
Last fall we were involved with the problem of Ontario corn. That was a serious situation. Of course the industry made representations and I must say, in all fairness, that the minister was most sympathetic. But for nine weeks the minister took no action. It is true that he caused meetings to be held. He did confer with officials in the United States where the corn was coming from which was causing us trouble. The minister made a deal with the United States whereby in exchange for the dropping of the duty on seven tariff items coming into Canada they would undertake to protect us from importation of cheap corn. Seven to one-that was not good enough. What the farmers and the people of the nation did not know was that the implementation of this protection in respect of corn would only be in effect for seven weeks. As of January 1 it expired. We are right back where we were. Unless action is taken immediately we will be in the same trouble this year.
Let us compare this situation with the actions other nations take against us. Whenever we encroach on the privileges and
May 1, 1969

rights of producers of other nations they do not wait weeks or months; they do not even wait for hours. When we go into their markets we find that, with perhaps an eight-hour warning, conditions are changed and we are faced with a tariff increase which means an almost complete ban on importation of our products. We on this side contend that it cannot always be that way. We believe that trade must be a two-way street. If we are treated in this fashion, surely we have the right to treat others in the same way. Why must our farmers always pay for the mistakes of others in respect of international agreements?
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I now come to the matter of credit. The only policy of any major proportion which the government has initiated in its entire life has been the increasing of credit to farmers. The increase of credit to farmers does not solve any of our major problems. All it does is increase their debt, increase land values, increase the value of the machinery they must buy, and place them in a position in which it is almost impossible to survive. And what does the government do? After initiating greater credit it established a policy, as it indicated in the house and at the congress, to put off the land what is calls inefficient and small farmers. Such a policy defeats the purpose for which credit was initiated in the first place.
Syndicate loans were supposed to be the answer. We were going to have larger corporate farms subsidized by government money which would be used to establish viable economic units. What does the implementation of the new estate tax do? It takes away the farmer's incentive to build up a corporate farm. This is why the farmers of this nation have no confidence in the government. This is why the farmers of this nation say that the government has no policy, or a confused policy. This is why the farmers of this nation cannot and will not make any money under these conditions. Surely the time is now for the government to act. Surely the government knows what is going on in the west and what is going on in the east. It knows how bad farmers' credit ratings are.
The farmers of this nation are sick to death of investigations, delegations, deliberations, conversations, and procrastination. Is it not time that we had some legislation? Even hon. members opposite must realize how serious the situation is and how urgent it is that solutions be applied now. This must be done
Business of Supply
if a great segment of the Canadian economy is not to fall into economic chaos and fade into oblivion. I commend this motion to hon. members.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on completion of what I wish to say in the new few minutes I will propose an amendment to the motion now before the house. But first I should like to say that I agree with the motion. I think it is time that we had a full discussion of the situation of Canadian farmers. The government and members on this side of the house must seriously consider the situation of the farmers, what is to be their place in the affairs of the nation and, perhaps even more important, whether some segments of the industry will have a place as owner-producers in this country.
One of the most important documents dealing with the situation of farmers in Canada was prepared by a group set up by the government of Ontario. Its title was, "The Challenge of Abundance". The challenge of abundance is really the challenge that faces the people of this nation in regard to farming and agriculture as we come to the end of the 1960's and in a few months move into the 1970's1. The problem is not that the farmer is unable to produce food as cheaply as he did 30 years ago. The fact of the matter is that he produces it for much less in terms of real and constant dollars. It is not that he does not have the know-how and the savvy. He is second to none anywhere in the world in his know-how, savvy, and understanding of the land, of the tools he uses, and of the economic climate in which he operates.
The real problem is to be found in the heading of the report to which I have referred-the challenge of abundance. The real problem is what our society is going to do with the knowledge, the know-how, the resources and the people we have at our beck and call. It is they who make us potentially one of the best fed nations in the world. I do not say that this is true for every Canadian. I suspect that as. I speak here this afternoon there are millions of Canadians who do not have all the food they want and all the proteins they need for their health. I suppose that there are many expectant mothers who do not have the food that is essential for their health. I suppose there are many children in this country who are not as well fed as those who live in well to do, middle class, homes. So there is this contrast. I will in no way

May 1, 1969
Business of Supply
attempt to describe what is happening in other parts of the world.
What is happening to our farmers as we face this challenge of abundance? One of the first things that happened after I came here as a member of the house last fall was the arrival of an array of tractors in front of the House of Commons, driven by the corn growers of Ontario. I spoke to some of their owners who were large producers. They do not lack the know-how with regard to the production of corn. What they sadly lack is a net income which would enable them to continue to operate effectively as producers.
As the previous speaker said, a solution has not been found. The representatives of the com growers are still making requests to appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture to state their position. I am sure they would not want to spend the time and effort to come here to appear before that committee unless their problems still existed. I suspect that in southern Ontario there is a a time bomb that will go off one of these days right in the lap of the government. Perhaps I am wrong; we will wait and see.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The Standing Committee on Agriculture has just returned from a trip to western Canada. We travelled right across that western land to Vancouver Island and we had an opportunity to see what was happening in the western part of this nation. I hope that in due course we shall do the same in the east. What did we see? We saw the same situation that was described in the Ontario report concerning the state of affairs in Ontario. We saw evidence of the challenge of abundance. People came before us representing the farming industry. Farmers came before us. I suspect that the tree fruits industry of British Columbia could produce a great deal more than it is producing at present. But the industry has organized supply management and is successfully maintaining a level of income for its people. We talked to very efficient egg producers. One of them had a blackboard upon which he put his costs. I believe the facts he put before us were true. I have been on many farms; he looked to me like an honest, family farm operator. He showed he was losing two cents a dozen on every dozen of eggs he moved off his farm.
We went to other places. We saw a barn with the number "8" on it. It was part of a factory operation. New forms of agriculture are developing today; we are moving into a

phase of factory operations. We were told about one concern which had plansi to move to the coast and set up a factory designed to produce 25,000 hogs per year. Mr. Speaker, we need a factory operation to produce hogs in Canada like we need a hole in the head. Farmers in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Quebec and the Maritimes have shown they are entirely capable of producing the amount of pork needed in Canada.
Then we came back and looked at the prairies. The house has been told of the situation which exists on the prairies. We split up into groups and went from farm to farm. We saw the actual situation there, not statistics.-[DOT] wheat piling up and not being moved to markets, farmers with inadequate incomes whose financial position made it doubtful that they could go ahead and put in another crop. What is worse, they really did not know what they should put in, what would be demanded of them by the people of Canada or the markets of the world. These farmers are operating in a no man's land so far as policy is concerned. The big question was: Where do we go from here?
I spoke of the challenge of abundance. I am convinced that we must develop a policy as a people which does not leave our farmers in a never-never-land wondering what their future is to be. I have often expressed concern about farm credit policies and the means by which young people can take up farming. But really, Mr. Speaker, the primary question is: Why should they? What is their future likely to be? Is it certain or uncertain? This is the real problem. The government and the people of Canada must realize that there is an emergency on the prairies as well as a situation which calls for long-term planning. The government must recognize that it cannot leave the problem as it now exists unanswered or regard it simply as a piece of unfinished business. We must produce both emergency and long-term solutions. Indeed, we have no choice.
The least we can do at the moment is establish a two-price system for wheat sold on the domestic market for human consumption so that farmers may receive a minimum of $3 per bushel for all wheat used in Canada for human consumption, and provide that the premium per bushed received over and above the International Grains Agreement price in the current crop year be distributed to all permit holders on the basis of the unit quota. This would at least recognize the fact that the grain farmer is a part of this nation and
May 1, 1969

entitled to treatment at least as good as that accorded to industry, which is protected by tariffs, or to the dairy industry which is protected by subsidies.
In addition, I believe we must recognize there is an emergency that must be dealt with immediately. Cash has to go into the hands of these farmers if they are to carry on business and if the social structure is not to collapse- I am thinking of the schools, roads and churches in the small communities of western Canada. There is much more at stake here than simply the livelihood and business operations of individual farmers.
The president of the Saskatchewan Farmers' Union stated in the west last week that it would take $175 million in federal aid to prevent the collapse of the grain industry in western Canada. I suspect he is right but I do not expect that the government will make such an amount available. I would have to be a flaming optimist to do so, having lived in the west and having watched this government for some time.
Nevertheless I should like to place before the house and the government the concrete proposal that as an emergency measure the government immediately make to all grain farmers an income deficiency payment of 20 cents a bushel on all wheat marketed in the 1967-68 grain crop year so as to put purchasing power in the hands of the farmers of western Canada. The maximum amount which any farmer might receive would be based on a 5,000 bushel delivery to the Canadian Wheat Board in the crop year to which I have referred. This policy should apply also to oats and barley in cases where a grower has delivered these grains rather than wheat.
This would not be enough but it would certainly help to meet the situation which is now at crisis point. I see in this chamber some of the men who toured Saskatchewan from farm to farm during the trip we made in the west, and they will surely agree with me. In the long term we shall be obliged to look at different solutions. We shall have to assess what the market actually is and study the channels open to us for the disposal of our wheat. I believe we should move away from the straight commercial approach we have followed up to now and turn to bilateral sales, to barter.
We must find out who needs this food and devise ways by which it may reach them. This means right here in Canada, in my book, and it applies also to those who live beyond our borders but who are none the less part of
Business of Supply
the human race. Hitler is supposed to have said that if he won the war and isolated North America, the people there would smother in their own fat. Unless we look outside our borders, we may do this. We are rich. But even rich people do not live alone; they have a host of other people to cater to their needs and serve them.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We must also be very concerned about the policy of the Canadian Dairy Commission in regard to the small dairy producers. Their needs are being neglected. They are being squeezed out. I have received letters from producers in my constituency asking for consideration of their problem, but according to the replies I have received from the commission this type of producer cannot be assisted under the regulations. I say to the government: This is not good enough.
I know one small grain producer in western Canada who is also a cow-calf man who produces some calves that go to feed lots in western Canada. He has to depend on his returns from the cream industry as well as from his calves in order to survive. Yet this state of affairs in western Canada today is being ignored. Representatives of the government of Manitoba attended one of the meetings of the standing committee and claimed that dairy producers were being discriminated against, that quotas were being transferred east.

interested in where quotas are transferred to. What interests me is that the needs of this type of producer are being totally ignored by the dairy commission. The Meadow Lake area is not just a grain producing area; neither is Saskatoon-Biggar. Let the government remember this and look at farming in its totality instead of following the bits and pieces approach that has unfortunately been taken up to now.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), the following subamendment:
That the motion be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "Canadian agriculture," the following words:
"which in the prairie provinces is due in the main to declining grain prices and reduced delivery quotas."

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on the non-confidence motion of the Progressive Conservative party, which reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this house the government has failed to deal with the seriously deteriorating net income of Canadian agriculture-
I would also like to talk about the amendment of the New Democratic party which refers to the situation of agriculture in the Prairies.
I shall deal with the subject in general, while acknowledging the merits of the amendment of the New Democratic party. The subject is a current issue in our regions. Had it been possible, we would have liked to add the following words to the amendment: and has neglected to recognize the right of farmers to be consulted about government policies which are always arrived at unilaterally.
As soon as the dairy policy of the current year was announced, I warned the minister that it would give rise to protests.
Today, Mr. Speaker, since our allotted time is 20 minutes, I will not refer to certain notes which I had jotted down, in order to deal exclusively with the protests. I will speak only about the farmers of my area.
In my opinion, the government has the obvious proof that the farmers are really unhappy, and rightly so, under the circumstances. We have heard that the farmers' income has decreased. This will not please them. If any producer were dealt with in this manner, strikes would necessarily occur.
Fortunately, farmers are not completely given to protests and do not react as others in various fields. I congratulate them for holding on. I hope that the government will finally review its position and that the commissioners of the Canadian Dairy Commission will take my comments into account, because I note that since the minister's last statements on the farm policy, nothing has changed.
It is impossible to exert any influence on the Canadian Wheat Board, and make it understand that there are some marginal cases. The only thing that matters is the administration of the law.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we shall have to use judgment as far as the interpretation of the legislation is concerned instead of enforcing it indiscriminately. It is rather easy to enforce a legislation; it is more difficult to
[Mr. Gleave.I
interpret it in such a way as to be fair with everyone.
Of course, we are the spokesmen of the farmers. They do send us their complaints. Some among them believe that we have the right to discuss the government policy. I shall point out to them that we do not have any more rights to do so than the back-benchers on the government side. The policy is all settled when it reaches us, without the opposition parties having been consulted. We are obliged to bear with the dictatorship of the department.
Then, when we go into our ridings, we are the ones who get it.
As a matter of fact, I have received so far more than 100 letters. I shall quote a few taken at random. They show not only to the minister but also to the Canadian Dairy Commission-since we are interested in industrial milk-the merits of our recommendations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity afforded by this debate today for two reasons. First, I think it is useful to have an opportunity provided to members of this house, after they have had a chance of assessing the situation with respect to agriculture, to give the government the benefit of their views as to what kind of policy, taking into account all of the consequences of adopting that policy and what would be most acceptable to the farming community. Second, I think it is useful because it is well for us to give consideration to the substance of the motion in such a way that we put it in perspective.
I know a little about this because I used to sit on the other side of the house. It is very easy to complain about everything without having to assume the responsibility for finding and administering solutions. I do not criticize members of the opposition, farm organizations or anyone else for taking that course, but I think it is fair and reasonable to say that when you have the responsibility for implementing policies you must look at the situation with a slightly different perspective.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say I concur in one statement that has been made so far in this debate, namely, the tremendous value of agriculture to the economy. There is no question in anyone's mind about that. We then go to the next stage and try to analyse the problem in sufficient depth so that we understand the root cause of the problem depressing the agricultural economy today.
I noted that the hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) borrowed the phrase, "the challenge of abundance", the task force in Ontario. I believe the greatest underlying reason for the present price structure and the low prices of many agricultural commodities in Canada today is the tremendous potential production in almost any commodity. It is so great, that whether it is cereals, dairy products, oil seeds or whatever, if there is an effort on the part of Canadian farmers to produce that product, in a very short time it will be in a surplus position which automatically damages the price structure. For some time after that we then continue to produce against the surplus. There are one or two commodities in the country that
May 1. 1969

are exceptions to that rule, but generally speaking I think it applies.
I am sure hon. members will agree we not only have a tremendous capacity to produce as much as there is effective demand for but substantially more than that. Indeed, this is what has happened in Canada with many commodities. I might also say it is not only in Canada that this has happened. If one looks at the figures compiled recently by the
O.E.C.D., one will see this production pattern taking place, in cereals and dairy products particularly, in many other countries of the world. The serious problem of over-production is also common to many fruits and vegetables. I wanted to say that at the outset, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want anyone to accuse me of saying that the farmers never had it so good. There are problems. We recognize those problems.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The motion this afternoon refers to "the seriously deteriorating net income for Canadian agriculture." It indicates that as a result farmers in all parts of Canada are "unable to obtain the necessary operating capital to finance the 1969-70 crop year." As I said, I think one would be less than realistic if one did not recognize that there are problems of farm income. These problems, of course, must be faced by agriculture from year to year, in many cases from commodity to commodity, depending on certain national aspects of the situation and also on the international context of affairs. However, to assert that farm income has seriously deteriorated and that Canadian farmers will be unable to finance their operations may, I suggest, in relation to recent history, not be quite consistent with the facts.
Unfortunately we do not have net farm income figures from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics for the first quarter of this year. However, we do have those for 1968, or at least we have a preliminary estimate. This estimate indicates that net farm income in Canada for 1968 will be about $170 million more than in 1967. In the absence of data in respect of farm income for the first quarter of this year, perhaps the best indicator of the present position of farmers is current farm prices. I am the first to admit that this is not always directly related to farm income, but I am sure hon. members will realize that there is a relationship. So I would like to place before the house certain information in respect of prices of various farm commodities in
Business of Supply
order that hon. members may judge for themselves whether the income situation is deteriorating in what is claimed is a serious, almost disastrous manner.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, the problem we get into is that I am sure that in any year since Confederation one could single out some commodity in some area, and sometimes more than one commodity in more than one area, and show that there was a very serious situation. But what I am trying to do in the few minutes I have available is to outline the whole of the picture, or as much of it as I can, respecting farm prices so that it will be in perspective.
Dealing first with livestock products, and I deal with them first simply because livestock and livestock products represent a total of 55 per cent of the income of farmers, as of today choice steers were selling in Toronto at $32.50 a hundredweight, up $3 or almost 10 per cent over a month ago, and up $5.20 per hundredweight over a year ago. I do not hear my hon. friends opposite cheering that, and at least that is something positive and good within the economy.

It states that an effort was made by the Australian Wheat Council and it has failed to agree on measures to restrict Australian wheat output to bring prices more in line with export demand. I am sure hon. members have read this story which is from the Financial Times of London. It reads in part as follows:
In the absence of concrete action the federal minister has appealed to farmers to exercise restraint. He said any grower would be foolish if he went blindly ahead without recognizing the problem of disposing of what he produced.

The United States has already reduced its wheat acreage allotment, and preliminary indications from Canada suggest that farmers have shown some restraint. However, without similar moves in Australia and Europe, a question mark must remain over the present international wheat price structure.

The Australian government last night announced its first wheat production restrictions as a result of the world glut and record Australian crops.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon in the short time allotted to me I intended to speak about some of the problems in western Canada, particularly in western agriculture, but after listening to the rosy picture painted by the minister I am wondering whether we are talking about the same part of Canada. In its recent tour of western Canada the Standing Committee on Agriculture heard expressed again and again what has been apparent to all western members for some time-the concern which exists in that part of the country today about the lack of grain sales and the corresponding desperate need for cash with which to carry on the necessary farm operations in the new crop year, operations which, by the way, will be commencing with the advent of spring weather.
The minister quoted figures to show that farm income for 1968 was reasonably high. He failed to mention that the cash advances last fall contributed to the income figure. He also mentioned that the number of cash advance payments made to the farmers last fall had doubled. The need for this money only proved that western agriculture is indeed experiencing a crisis. To compound the problem, this spring the final payments on wheat, oats and barley were almost the smallest ever. They will not be sufficient to pay the grocery bills from the first of January until the time farmers receive their cheques.
Because of the glut of wheat on the farms and in the elevators of the country our farmers have been advised by the task force on agriculture to switch their production from wheat to other crops. To our harried farmers this advice poses some serious problems. First, there is the very real danger that in switching to other crops they will only compound the problem by producing embarrassing surpluses in other cereal grains. Second, by reducing in favour of other than cereal grains wheat acreage, the quota on which the farmer may deliver his wheat is reduced, making it even more difficult for him to reduce the surplus wheat which he already has in store.
Business of Supply
In view of the assistance which farmers have rendered the national economy by providing a much needed balance of payments in our foreign exchange, particularly in 1963 when, according to the Governor of the Bank of Canada, they thus averted an economic crisis-I think the foreign exchange thus gained amounted to $480 million or more- and in further consideration of the loss of wheat delivery quota that would result from any reduction of wheat acreage that is sown in other than cereal crops, surely it is incumbent upon the government at this time to assist farmers in their efforts to reduce the wheat acreage. This can be done, as has been done in the past, by a wheat acreage reduction payment. It can be achieved by making a payment to the farmers for each acre on which wheat is not sown, based on the 196768 permit book record, up to a maximum which the government considers necessary to achieve a wheat crop of manageable proportions. At the same time this would provide the farmers with necessary funds to help finance their spring operations. The land taken out of wheat production would either have to be left fallow or be sown to grass or forage crops in order to achieve this objective.
I feel that this action is not only justified on the basis of past experience but essential to the national well-being in that many of our competent farmers are being forced to the wall because of their inability to finance on a six-bushel quota that is now extended to a two-year period. With large stocks of unsold grain upon which cash advances were taken in order to pay harvest expenses, our farmers are entering a new crop season with their hands tied for lack of working capital.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I hope the government will give consideration to the proposal I have put forward, one which has been endorsed by farm leaders and farm organizations as a means of bringing temporary assistance to our farmers and of enabling them to finance the production of this year's crop. At the same time, I wish to point out that the regaining of our lost share of the world wheat market must remain the primary objective not only of our wheat marketing agencies but of the government itself. After all, it is the government which has the power not only to bring some flexibility to our marketing program but also to allow extensions of credit which could make all the difference in effecting sales. At best, the wheat

acreage reduction payment proposal could be regarded only as an interim provision designed to assist western agriculture to maintain the stability necessary to overcome a period of extreme stress.
Having regard to the mounting cost of farm operations because of inflation, something for which the Canadian farmer can in no way be held responsible, I believe it is not only fair but in the best interests of the nation that further continuing compensation be provided to our farmers for helping to bear the brunt of the government's cheap food policy. There are many ways in which this can be done by means of government action. Surely the government has people who are smart enough to figure out ways and means of assisting our farmers through this difficult period. If not, it is time they allowed someone else to run the country.
The government should take another look at the value of our special crops in terms of reducing wheat acreage, and should provide the oilseed industry with long overdue protection against the flow of cheap vegetable oil and oilseed entering this country at prices which bear no relationship to the cost of production. This situation could be resolved by placing on the imported product either a value comparable with that placed on United States cottonseed oil or, as an absolute minimum, one equal to the Canadian price for soya beans. Sunflower seed growers in Manitoba and soya bean growers in Ontario will then have at least a chance to compete with a foreign product which is obviously being delivered in Canada at prices below an acceptable cost of production.
The hardship at present being experienced on the prairies is not just a figment of someone's imagination, and I am sure the minister must be aware of this despite the rosy picture he has painted. For the benefit of his colleagues' in the government I think I should emphasize that a combination of circumstances beyond the control of our farmers has created a situation in which many of those engaged in agriculture in the west find themselves in a precarious position.
Briefly, these circumstances were as follows: First, there was a disastrous loss of markets which left Canadian producers with 20 per cent of the export market whereas they had previously held 40 per cent. Favourable whether conditions throughout the world's wheat producing countries and, indeed, in countries which do not normally enter the export market, added millions of

bushels to the world wheat surplus. An unusually wet harvest caused further problems for Canadian farmers inasmuch as an estimated 350 million bushels of grain were harvested in a tough or damp condition. Our farmers did a Herculean job attempting to dry their grain, assisted to some extent by the grain handling facilities made available to them. There is no doubt, however, that a significant amount of this out of condition grain was lost as a result of spoilage, particularly in areas where frost had affected the quality. The cost of handling this, grain has been out of proportion to usual harvesting expenses and has added a further burden to an industry short of cash.
For six long months, representatives of our national farm organizations, federal members, provincial premiers and other western leaders have been seeking an assurance from the government that something would be done to alleviate the effects of hardship on the prairies owing to loss of grain sales. Time is now running out for those farmers who desperately need help to finance their spring operations. Surely the minister will not shrug this off as opposition propaganda.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on this motion. Statements have been made recently both inside and outside the house to the effect that the government is showing indifference and disregard with respect to farmers and agriculture in Canada. I should like to take a few moments in which to set the record straight. The time spent in this house on agriculture since the session began last September amounts to more than has been spent on any other sector of our economy or on any other subject. The debate today only continues this tradition.
We have passed a lot of legislation having to do with agriculture. I can name many of these measures. There was the measure providing for increased cash advances, and the figure was then raised for the special purpose of enabling farmers to dry grain. There was the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Farm Credit Corporation Act, the Farm Syndicates Credit Act, the measures concerned with pests and pesticide control and compensation to farmers for losses caused through the contamination of their crops or animals.
As a farmer and a private member on the government side of the house I think it is incumbent on me to draw attention to some of the services and assistance which are being provided on a continuing and in many cases an expanding basis for the farmers of Canada. A few of these services, I am quick to admit, were instituted by Conservative governments during those brief periods since 1930 in which the people of Canada entrusted them with the affairs of our country. But most of them were initiated by Liberal governments and are being continued and improved by the present government. Most fair-minded farmers will, I believe, be willing to agree that this is so.
I believe the Liberal government is guilty of not doing a better job of letting people know what has been done and what is being done. May I take just a minute or two, Mr. Speaker, to set out some of the services and assistance now being provided to the farmers of Canada.
They include a tremendous program of research and information, the inspection and grading of new products, marketing and production research, the programs of pest and disease control. The prices of a variety of products, including wool, eggs and hogs, have been stabilized at a cost of about $140 million a year if one includes the dairy division. There is the Canadian Livestock Feed Board
29180-522J
Business of Supply
which protects both our livestock and the feed grain industry. The Wheat Board has now been placed on a permanent basis as the result of the action of the Liberal government. The Board of Grain Commissioners provides services connected with the grading and inspection of our grain. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act provides assistance to farmers who have suffered partial or complete crop failure, to an average cost of about $9 million a year.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Then there is P.F.R.A. which provides for irrigation, community pasture projects, dams and so on. There is crop insurance, on which the federal government pays half the administration costs and 25 per cent of the premium costs. Then there are grants to a multitude of agricultural associations, such as the seed growers, the 4-H movement, livestock associations, plowing associations, various fairs and what have you. This represents a total expenditure of at least $300 million per year by way of assistance to farmers in all parts of the country.
Then there is the Canada Grains Council which was recently established by the government and which I think augers well for the future. Then there is the Canadian Congress on Agriculture and, last but not least, the tour of the western provinces just concluded by the agricultural committee of the House of Commons.
Then we have the emergency wheat reserves legislation which last year put at least $37 million into the coffers: of the Wheat Board. Over the years it has put in amounts varying from 5.9 cents a bushel to 12.9 cents a bushel. These payments have been made ever since the Liberal party inaugurated that program in 1956 under the wheat reserves act. This year there was also put into the coffers of the Wheat Board at least $7 million on account of the support the government provided for the price of wheat during the 11 month period in 1967-68 when there was no effective international grains arrangement. If you add those two figures together, Mr. Speaker, a sum of at least $44 million or $45 million has been provided compared with the total final payment on wheat to the farmers of $60 million. In other words, if it had not been for those two payments to the Wheat Board in 1967-68, the final payment on wheat last month would have been not 12 5 cents a bushel but 4 or 5 cents a bushel.

speechtext:
This storage payment comes from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada, as does the floor price for wheat which cost $7 million.
The motion before us refers to the deteriorating net income of Canadian farmers. I hope you will forgive me, Mr. Speaker, if I refer in particular to the severe financial crisis in western agriculture but that is the area with which I am most familiar, one in which I think I can claim some experience and, I hope, at least a little knowledge.
Let me first outline some of the events leading up to the present situation. Farm marketings of wheat for export have varied a great deal in the past ten years, from the crop year 1958-59 to 1967-68 inclusive. In the first five years of that period exports of wheat and flour averaged 323 million bushels per year. During the next four years the average was 520 million bushels per year. Last year, the tenth year in this period, exports dropped to 335 million bushels.
On the strength of the forecasts and predictions made over the past several years by Canadian and international food experts, economists, government officials and politicians of various political parties, grain farmers have increased their efficiency in the production of grain. They have enlarged their units to make them more economical. They have purchased larger and more modern machinery and have built new and better grain storage facilities. In so doing, and on the strength of the advice that they received, many of them have gone into debt. Now, as a result of reduced markets, falling prices and rising costs, they find themselves unable to meet their debt obligations in a great many cases. They also find themselves short of cash to pay their operating expenses.
At one time farm requirements were relatively small. Merchants and machinery dealers 40 or 50 years ago used to extend credit to the farmers, and this helped them to finance their most modest requirements. This is no longer possible. The service industry has been forced to go on a cash basis to a large extent. Farm inputs have a much wider variety and a much greater volume now. I believe it is incumbent on the people of Canada to come to the rescue of our food producers and the industry that has contributed and does contribute far more to Canada than the ratio that its numerical proportion has to our

national economy, as well as to our export trade. Agriculture is still one of Canada's most important industries, and maintaining this industry in a healthy condition is essential in order to keep our national economy from faltering, as history shows is the inevitable result of depressed conditions in the agricultural sector.
Before I enumerate some suggestions I should like to make, may I briefly expand on one suggestion. I refer to the so-called two-price system for wheat. I believe there is an overwhelming argument in favour of some such system which would give farmers a fairer return on at least that part of wheat production that is used for domestic human consumption. Other sectors of the economy, such as the manufacturers, professional people and labour, have effective methods of increasing their incomes, but these methods are not available to the farmers. Wheat prices are very little higher than they were 20 years ago, whereas the price of commodities and services required by the farmers has practically doubled in the same period. Therefore a special domestic price for wheat is amply justified.
There are, however, some possible difficulties associated with such a two-price system. For example, there is the possibility of our being accused of dumping. Other countries might impose sanctions on Canadian exports in other sectors of our economy if they successfully proved that we were dumping our agricultural products or selling them in other markets at a lower figure than we sell them at home.
There is also the question of bread imports. At the present time I am given to believe that in certain cities near the United States border U.S. bread sells at less than the price of Canadian bread. If we increase our bread prices and the United States does not, there will be a problem to be faced there. We might also expect to have policing problems with a two-piece wheat system, with a price differential of $1, so far as millers and other processors are concerned. In addition, the costs of administration naturally go up because a two-price system would have to be carefully administered. There would also be what to my mind is the most serious problem of deciding how to distribute the proceeds of a two-price system for wheat. I do not think the wheat producers themselves have agreed on how the proceeds should be distributed among them.
May 1. 1969

I have consistently spoken in favour of a two-price system for wheat at every opportunity, especially since I became involved in federal politics about a year ago. In my first speech in the house I called on the government to give early and sympathetic consideration to some such system of paying the wheat farmers a fair price for domestic wheat. I have mentioned this many times since and I renew my plea today.
My first suggestion, which is most necessary in order to find both a long and a short term solution to the farm income problem, is that sales efforts by all agencies concerned with marketing farm products should be increased by making maximum use of all selling techniques in both the domestic and export markets. To that end the government should support and strengthen the Wheat Board system of marketing by making whatever legislative changes may be necessary to allow the Canadian Wheat Board to expand its export sales.

speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members. I suggest that the government support the floor price of wheat at the level of the minimums of the International Grains Arrangement. I suggest also that the government introduce a wheat acreage reduction program which would compensate farmers reducing their wheat acreage, with greater incentive to be given to those who convert that acreage to pasture and for the growing of forage crops. Greater incentives should also be given to farmers farming in areas in which grades of wheat low in protein are produced. Also, the government should provide farmers with higher returns for wheat used for human consumption in Canada by authorizing the Canadian
Business of Supply
Wheat Board to charge higher prices for such wheat or by such other methods as will achieve the same result.
As an interim measure to help in alleviating the current shortage of operating funds, I suggest that the government consider making an immediate payment of ten cents per bushel, in lieu of the two price system, on wheat delivered in the 1967-68 crop year. As hon. members will see, I am less optimistic than was the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) who mentioned 20' cents per bushel. I suggest that the immediate payment ought to be ten cents per bushel, with a minimum payment of $250 to any farmer and a maximum of $500 per bona fide farm operator.
My further suggestions are that the government institute a special program of assistance on an interim basis to farmers operating small, uneconomic units; that the government provide for more research into the problems of agricultural markets and forecasting as well as into the problems of alternate uses for farm products; that the government continue and expand its support for credit sales of farm products; that the government take steps to prevent any increase in the tolls charged on the St. Lawrence seaway; that the government consider the advisability of placing the Canadian Wheat Board under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture and that the Wheat Board be asked to review the operation of its quota system with a view to making it more equitable and effective.
I shall suggest, too, that the government ought to take steps to insure the equitable distribution of box cars and the best possible use of our grain handling and transportation system; that the government continue to promote the improvement and use of the Hudson Bay route; that the government investigate the alleged dumping of vegetable oil on the Canadian market and take the necessary action to prevent it, and that the government take all necessary action to restrain rising costs and prices of products and services used in agricultural production.
My other recommendations are that the government take steps to provide for some direct producer representation on the Canadian Wheat Board and that the creditors extend extra time to farmers required to repay loans made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Farm Credit Corporation Act. Of course, I am speaking of those farmers who will find it difficult to meet their payments this spring. These suggestions,

Mr. Speaker, may or may not form part of the recommendations contained in an early report of the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
My concluding remarks, Mr. Speaker, are to tell hon. members that an emergency situation is facing Canadian agriculture.
