speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was1 very happy to learn that today's sitting would be spent on a discussion of agricultural problems and especially of the Canadian farmers' situation.
I hope that our discussion, which I trust will be objective, will lead to some solutions, so that farmers may have the security to which they are entitled and to which they have aspired for a long time.
We have already heard the comments of several government members on the matter. We are told repeatedly that the government is trying to do something, that its intentions are of the best. The situation was the same seven or eight months ago. The speeches will go on, and the previous speaker will again take the floor. As a matter, of fact, he does' not in the least think that the government has done nothing. In his opinion, it has accomplished a great deal. I agree, of course, that a government is always elected to do something.

I suggest we should ask: has the government done enough? Can it do more and better? Even with the best intentions in the world, we remain convinced that what has been done is not enough. This is obvious when we study the farmers' situation.
I will be told: This is not easy, or; we have problems. But should we let things as they are just because there is no easy solutions? Should we let matters take care of themselves in due time? Should we be satisfied by simply saying that it is difficult?
As a member from eastern Canada, and more particularly from the province of Quebec, I hope that other Quebec M.P.'s, especially those on the government side, will take advantage of this day not only to recommend to the government to do something but also to compel it to act.
One could say that, from time to time, during the meetings of the caucus, members speak louder and express their viewpoints. But I think we have today a special opportunity to tell the government what the farmers need. I believe the people are expecting that not only opposition members but government members as well will put forward strong and specific proposals whereby farm people would be appreciated once and for all and would get the recognition to which they are entitled.
Considering that one third of the Canadian labour force is related directly or indirectly to farming and has to work under intolerable conditions at the present time, and considering also that the situation is disastrous for the national economy, I think we must find solutions to the problem and ensure that they will have lasting results.
The present problems are somewhat similar to those that prevailed four or five years ago. Travelling across Canada, one finds the same conditions everywhere. No doubt that production costs have considerably increased but income is not much higher, so we are finally faced with overproduction.
I would find it hard to understand that a country as well known as ours where the workers are willing, generally, to work towards their common goal, would let 30 per cent of its population live in poverty while it experiences overproduction it is unable to consume as it should in its best interests.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I have already said and I repeat it that there were problems of consumption and production in Canada.
May 1, 1969

In my opinion, if the government must make any effort, it must try to find some formula for the consumption of that production. It will also have to consider reviewing the matter of our imports. We should also perhaps ask the government to adopt another philosophy and compel it to act differently.
It will surely have to assert itself a little more forcibly from time to time, as far as high finance is concerned. Some agreements concerning imports were concluded a few years ago and as a result of some developments, it would be advisable to review those agreements. We are back from a trip in the West. Once more we noticed that there is overproduction in that region. Both the East and the West have similar problems, that is the cost of production and income.
Because of the importance of that industry in Canada, I feel that the government should now have a guarantee policy. It should guarantee the purchase of our production and find outlets for it. Maybe the role played by the agencies which promote the sale of our products abroad should be revised. Above all, we must ensure the security of our producers.
It is now impossible, since all the hon. members who made the trip acquainted themselves with the problems of farming, not to appreciate those facts.
In the circumstances, it would be useless for me or for the other hon. members to discuss that problem for weeks. It was said a while	ago	that much	time	hasbeen devoted	to	agriculture	since	thebeginning of	this	session. In	fact,	we
have been content with wasting our time. We have passed some pieces of legislation, we have found a formula allowing our farmers to borrow on a larger scale, to get deeper into debt. They will need a long period of time to pay back their loans. We found it enough to grant them five or six extra years to reimburse the money borrowed. I do not think it fair. That is not the proper way to provide help to our farmers.
The government should establish a guaranteed price policy. I have already suggested that without any results. I had thought that we might be able to help our producers in getting labour from the Unemployment Insurance office, without depriving the unemployed from their unemployment benefits. This measure would enable the producers to get cheap labour, which would, by the way, reduce production costs.
Business of Supply
It had been felt that the idea was not so bad after all, but, I have not heard about it since.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that together we should find a solution with the sole purpose of giving back to the farmers the guarantee and the security they need.
I do not believe that in view of the importance of the question, the present government can hesitate longer.
I still believe in the objectivity of everyone of those who represent the ridings of Canada. Thus, with a firmer and more objective attitude, thanks to this day of debate, which has allowed us to study the problem together and to find rapidly a solution, the minister will be able to announce us shortly what steps he intends to take and the farmers will be satisfied.

Mr. Speaker, one of the purposes of this debate is to try to obtain from the government benches some indication of their opinion of the condition of Canadian agriculture at this time, and in particular the state of agriculture in western Canada. In this respect, the debate so far has been very confusing. Two members of the Liberal Party have spoken. One said he conceded agriculture in western Canada was in a state of emergency or crisis. The minister said he would consider the situation as "I wouldn't want to say the farmers never had it so good". This isi a grudging admission by the minister that perhaps there is a small problem.
If the minister wants my opinion as to what the situation is, I say without fear of exaggeration that it is one of crisis proportions. Surely, the minister must be aware of that. The minister does not have to take only the word of members on this side of the house. He can ask his colleague from Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) or some of his colleagues who toured western Canada with the Committee on Agriculture. I recall that two weeks ago when the Wheat Board representatives appeared before the committee, two members from eastern Canada said in so many words that they considered the situation facing western farmers to be tragic and one of emergency. Those were the words they used. Surely, they must have meant what they were saying, unless they were playing to the press gallery.
The minister should admit it is time the government took some concrete action and

presented to parliament some specific proposals on how to meet this serious situation. Earlier this afternoon, the minister put on the record certain figures indicating the number of farmers who were taking cash advances in western Canada. I will be one of the first to say that the cash advance legislation introduced by the Conservative government in the late fiftiesi was a very worth-while piece of legislation. I think hon. members of the Conservative party will acknowledge that the C.C.F. had also been trying to impress on a former Liberal government of the late fifties that such legislation should be implemented. It was incredible that the minister would cite the figures showing how much had been taken up in cash advances as something of which to be proud. To me, that is one of the best means of showing there is a serious cash position on the prairies. The more that is taken by way of cash advances, the more we should be worrying and shuddering about the prospects for repayment.
The number of farmers in Manitoba who took advantage of the cash advance legislation last year was very small. This year, I am informed the number of farmers who have taken out cash advances has increased by a factor of 10, ten times as many as was the case in preceding years. To me, that is a sign

of danger. The minister should not point to that as a defence.
I realize part of the problem facing agriculture in the west has to do with declining international sales, plugged markets and declining prices. I suggest to the minister there are some specific steps that should be taken. The government must try to help the Canadian Wheat Board in its task of promoting the sale of Canadian wheat. I suggest the sales staff of this organization should be supplemented. How many men are actually engaged as salesmen exclusively of the Canadian Wheat Board? It is a very small number. The number should be increased, either directly under the aegis of the Wheat Board or indirectly by using Canadian trade personnel at Canadian trade bureaus overseas as supplementary agents of the Wheat Board.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
At a time of crisis, that is the least that should be done. For how long are we going to continue with a state of affairs in which the actual transactions for our entire export sales of wheat are dependent upon five or six international concerns? The minister knows to which ones I am referring-the Dreyfus Corporation, the Bungy Corporation, the Carghill Corporation of Minneapolis, and one or two others. To them, it is of little concern whether they are handling Canadian wheat or some other country's. The government has not taken the initiative to see that a Canadian corporation is established that would become engaged in precisely this kind of work. I suggest this should be done.
There is nothing to stop the minister from impressing upon his cabinet colleagues the seriousness of the situation, and the amount of money required to tide the prairie economy over this most difficult of times. There is nothing to stop him from getting the agreement of his colleagues to assist whatever entrepreneurship exists in Canada to set up an international trading agency.
I am sure the minister has enough facts and figures to back up his case. Why isn't he doing it? He is not in a weak position. He is one of the few Liberal cabinet ministers from the prairies. He is one of the few Liberal members of parliament from the prairies, and his colleagues must surely know that unless he is given some co-operation and authority there will be even fewer after the next election.
There is one other matter which I must refer to at this time. It is the way in which

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate and second the motion of nonconfidence in the government on its agricultural policies, or I should say lack of policies,
Business of Supply
I wish to point out that I do so in all seriousness. There are many emergencies in Canada today. One can think of the housing situation and the recent resignation of the former Minister of Transport over lack of government action. I want to suggest that if immediate action is not forthcoming then the Minister or Agriculture (Mr. Olson) had better resign too. Then, perhaps the government will come to life.
Look at the unemployment situation, at the high cost of living, the water and air pollution problems, postal services and many others. But paramount and most important is the emergency facing our economy in the field of agriculture. Just recently our Standing Committee on Agriculture made a tour of the four western provinces. Some 35 briefs were presented to us, including representations from the premiers or ministers of agriculture of the western provinces. At this point I would like to congratulate in particular the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool on organizing one of the most effective tours of Saskatchewan with regard to agriculture for committee members, and on the work it did in bringing farmers' problems to the attention of the committee.
Not only did we hold meetings in some of the major cities, but we also went out to farm homes where representative farmers were even prepared to open up their books, show us their income tax statements, and demonstrate in general the standard of their economy. If nothing else beneficial came from this there was the effect of the tour on Liberal members of the committee who had been criticizing us for being too vociferous, and sometimes too partisan, over the past several months in bringing agricultural problems to their attention. This tour made them finally realize that there was a basis for our complaints. As we went from place to place, it was interesting to note the sympathy that developed in their minds for our points of view and for the problems facing western Canada.
I should now like to quote one or two passages from the brief prepared for the committee by the Hon. W. Ross Thatcher, Premier of Saskatchewan, whose comments I think are important because of his political affiliation. They give positive proof of the position of western farmers.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, my contribution will be short in keeping with the rules we have agreed upon. In his brief the Premier of Saskatchewan said:
The economic circumstances of a majority of prairie producers are desperate.
He referred to loss of sales and said:
The farmer's first problem is caused by an inability to market a large proportion of his grain.
He went on to state:
Presently quotas at most elevator points are the lowest in a decade. Thus the cash position of the farmer is extremely serious.
On the prairies, we must literally market or perish.
All the briefs received by the committee indicated that never before has the cost-price squeeze taken such a firm hold on our farmers. Some underlying causes are; (1) loss of markets, and particularly the temporary lapse of the International Wheat Agreement which brought about this serious situation; (2) high cost of machinery and repairs; (3) higher taxes; (4) lower farm prices; (5) tight quotas and low sales; (6) the burden of drying huge piles of damp grain; (7) higher interest rates.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The eighth cause, to add insult to injury, is the new Estate Tax Act. In fact, it was startling to note, in a recent position paper the task force prepared for the agricultural congress that completed its four day conference several weeks ago at the Chateau Laurier here in Ottawa, that the net income, on the basis of the average capital investment, for the farmer in Canada for the last full year under review was only 1.32 per cent. Putting it another way, it represents a return of only 40 cents per man-hour of labour to the farmer.
I was never one to criticize without making some specific suggestions to improve a situation. Therefore, I should like to make a few

suggestions. These are some I have already outlined to the chairman of the agricultural committee who was with us on our recent journey across western Canada.
My first suggestion is it is my belief that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), accompanied by the Ministers of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), Agriculture, (Mr. Olson), and possibly External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), together with several advisors from each of their departments, should immediately journey to Washington to have an emergency discussion with their counterparts with a view to setting machinery in motion to see to it that the terms of the recent International Grain Agreement be activated to the full.
I make this suggestion in all seriousness because our great neighbour to the south, during the Kennedy Round discussions several years ago in Geneva, was instrumental in persuading usi to allow the wheat agreement to lapse. Then, they were the first offenders when in August 1967 they dumped a large amount of grain into some of our traditional markets at 22 cents below the agreed price. I think this was a gross violation. I think they should co-operate now by being the first to help us initiate this new world agreement.
My second suggestion is- that various trade policies should be developed by our own Department of Trade and Commerce with respect to the sale of wheat such as long term, low interest credit arrangements, especially to emerging nations, and reciprocal trade agreements with prospective or current importers of our wheat.
Thirdly, I believe a close examination should be made at once of our Board of Grain Commissioners grading formula with a view to bringing it into line with the grading practices. of our competitors and demands of our importers.
The fourth suggestion is that, as an immediate one year emergency measure, acreage payments should be made to the farmers under the quota and permit book system similar to the action taken in 1958, 1959 and 1961. A maximum of $60 million should be allotted for this purpose. This would assist a farmer in buying needed seed in those areas of the west where his crop was frozen or supplement the purchase of fuel or other necessities for spring planting.
As my fifth suggestion, I believe the principle of a two-price system should be inaugurated at once. This would supplement the temporary acreage payment in the future and
May 1, 1969

the benefits from it would begin to be felt in the agricultural economy next year.
My sixth suggestion is that serious consideration should be given to establishing a fully Canadian based commodity sales organization to handle, on behalf of the Wheat Board, our wheat, oatsi, barley and rye, flax and rape seed for that matter, rather than depend on the several major commission houses situated in the United States and Europe that presently carry on this business for us.
I suggest as the seventh point that a transport controller or co-ordinator be appointed who would see to it that the agricultural industry got its fair share of the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National rolling stock in times of emergency, similar to that which we experienced this fall and winter in moving grain to the west coast.
Suggestion number eight isi: Consideration might be given to the establishment of one or two terminal elevators in Europe and Asia of reasonable grain carrying capacity which would provide storage for grain that would be readily accessible for the market, should speedy delivery be a factor in making a sale.
Suggestion number nine is that marketing research should be greatly activated.
I could go on to mention a number of others, but because my time is limited I shall conclude with this suggestion. I think if these suggestions were effected we would have a greatly improved industry. What concerns our farmers, in a state of sorrow and disbelief, is the apparent indifference to their plight. Liberal speeches always seem to leave the implication that the farmers never had it so good. An example was the speech by the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon and that of his colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia, (Mr. Douglas), although the latter in closing his remarks did admit there is an emergency in agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate today concerning agriculture because of the concern I feel for this industry and this way of life in Canada.
Recently I took part in the tour of western Canada by the Committee on Agriculture during which we visited agricultural areas and saw many facets of this industry in the four western provinces. I should like to point out that this visit was to the grass roots level of agriculture in western Canada and that it was approved by the government. I believe that many of the cries which we hear that the government is not concerned with the problems of the people of western Canada, and of farmers, is just not true. The government members of this committee took an active part in the western tour, and I think it needs

May 1, 1969
Business of Supply
to be pointed out and emphasized, that it was the Liberal government that approved and encouraged this trip.

If the government were not concerned with the problems of western Canada, I can assure you that they would never have agreed to the visit by the standing Committee on Agriculture because this visit draws attention to the problems in agriculture.
In our trip to western Canada, I was particularly impressed by the diversification of agriculture that we saw in Alberta. Although grain farming is an important part of this industry in that province, agriculture there is generally much more diversified than in Saskatchewan. Dairying, beef farms, hog and poultry production as well as cash crops such as sugar beet, make for a more balanced agriculture in that province.
We visited the Kinsella experimental farm where important experiments in genetics are being carried out to develop more hardy strains of beef producing animals. These experiments are also aimed at improving the conversion factor of feed to beef. At Lacombe in southern Alberta we visited the federal government experimental farm where the federal government has spent millions of dollars over the last half a century to aid western agriculture. I say to the opposition: Is this the kind of federal government aid to agriculture in which you have no confidence?
Federal government aid to research has always been an important key to improved production. Surely, the members of the opposition who travelled with this committee cannot be voting against the federal government's policy of increasing aid to research in the production of better cereal grains. In British Columbia, the standing Committee on Agriculture visited the terminal elevators where millions of bushels of wheat are shipped annually to the Pacific rim countries of Japan and China.
At the Saskatchewan Pool elevators we saw a Toyota ship tied up which wasi loading wheat for Japan. A few days previously this ship had come from Japan loaded with a cargo of Toyota cars, and I think we should realize that trade is a two way street. Our foreign customers must sell to us in order to be able to buy from us. Perhaps we should spend a little time considering whether the jokes we make about small foreign cars are

really appropriate in this day when we so desperately need world sales of wheat, especially to the countries that make small cars such as Japan, Germany and England.
In British Columbia, I was most impressed with the way the producers of agricultural products such as milk, eggs, broilers and orchard crops have organized their production and marketing more efficiently than in any other place I know in Canada. The term "supply management" was one that we heard most often in British Columbia, and perhaps this is the key to the future success of agriculture in Canada. We are a country that can produce a surplus of agricultural products beyond what we can consume ourselves or what we can sell on the foreign markets. I believe that the future success and stability of the agricultural industry in Canada depends on supply management, so that we produce what we can sell and we sell at a fair price which will reward the producer adequately for his labour and investments.
This is not to say that there are no problems in agriculture in British Columbia. We heard many briefs in this province, and the Committee on Agriculture will be making recommendations on these problems to the House of Commons and to the government. Perhaps the most important part of this trip was our visit to Saskatchewan because this is the province that produces a major share of Canadian wheat. The biggest problem lies in over-production of wheat and insufficient sales on the foreign market, coupled with excess moisture in last fall's crop.
I must congratulate the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which organized for the 30 committee members some 24 meetings in small towns across the province which were attended by some 18,000 farmers. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool field men were excellent hosts for the committee members and organized every detail of the tour in that province most satisfactorily. Not only did the committee members meet hundreds of farm people at formal meetings but they visited as well individual farmers to review their problems right on the farms. I visited farms where 30,000 bushels of wheat were stored.

The economic circumstances of a majority of prairie producers are desperate.
The farmers' first problem is caused by an inability to market a large proportion of his grain.
For the past several years, export sales have fallen off sharply. As a result, in the last crop year, farmers were only able to deliver six bushels per acre.
I understand that for the year previous to the last crop year deliveries were down to three bushels. The quotas are even lower now.
I continue quoting from the brief:
On the prairies, we must literally market or perish. We call on the federal government to take every conceivable step, to increase foreign sales.
In particular, we ask for an extension of export credit facilities.
The brief then referred to the cost-price squeeze:
The second problem of the prairie farmer is caused by the so-called cost-price squeeze.
Mr. Chairman, since the end of the war, annually throughout Canada, there has been a consistent upward trend in prices, wages and incomes. Year after year, sharp wage increases have been demanded and given, to virtually every union handling the farmers' products.
-	the longshoremen
-	the railroaders
-	the maritime unions
-	the dock workers
-	the elevator operators, and so on.
One such settlement a few years ago, gave 30 per cent in one contract, to the longshoreman-[DOT] and they have had substantially more since that time. Many of these wage increases were given after direct intervention, persuasion and pressure by the federal government. In every case, the farmer has been obliged to absorb a substantial portion of these huge wage increases. I think it should be realized by the committee, that in Saskatchewan since 1949, average wages and salaries have increased 146 per cent. The cost of machinery and other basic materials which the farmer must buy has doubled, in the same period-
But while all this has been happening, the farmers' selling price for wheat has remained almost static... In other words, at a time when inflation and escalating costs have never been so serious, the farmer has had virtually no increased returns. The result of course has been, that thousands of our farmers have been obliged to leave farming. Thousands of others are caught in an economic squeeze, that monthly becomes more desperate ... Mr. Chairman, the very basis of the prairie economy is agriculture. We do not believe that the nation is treating the wheat farmer fairly.

When we were in British Columbia I was happy to be able to move a motion that affects Ontario farmers even more than it affects British Columbia farmers. It had to do with equalizing the tariff on eviscerated or dressed poultry and live poultry which is coming into this country at an increasing rate. I understand that Professor Cavers, the former head of the poultry department at the University of Guelph-and his opinions are respected throughout Canada-thinks that United States producers are gearing up to send increasing quantities of live poultry into Canada. They will do so because the tariff on live poultry is only two cents whereas on eviscerated poultry it is five cents. The standing Committee on Agriculture approved my motion unanimously, and agreed that this matter ought to be brought to the government's attention in order that immediate action might be taken. Such action would increase the two-cent tariff on fowl, broilers, turkeys, and poultry to 4 cents, equal to that on dressed poultry.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I am happy to know the Standing Committee on Agriculture is going to tour eastern Canada later this year, because everything is not rosy in this part of the country. I shudder to think what will happen to eastern agriculture if the western farmers, in order to get grain markets, feed all their grain to livestock. What will happen to eastern agriculture? Eastern farmers will be out of business, yet that is what western farmers are doing at the present time.
The eastern farmers have many millions of dollars invested in efficient equipment to handle this job. They are doing a tremendous job. If the western farmer is forced, through lack of grain sales caused by the ineffectiveness of the present government, to feed this grain to livestock the eastern farmers will be in serious trouble. If this happens, it will only be a matter of two or three years until the other segments of the economy are affected. This has been proven down through history.
Some people say only between 7 and 9 per cent of the people are employed in agriculture. I think in the production of agricultural products, processing, distributing and all down the line, approximately 40 per cent are engaged in agriculture. If agricultural products are brought in from other countries,

either frozen or canned, 40 per cent of the people in this country will be unemployed.
I plead with the government to take action at the present time to avoid a future disaster. A small amount of action and real consideration of this problem will prevent any serious consequences that might be ahead for this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member from a Quebec constituency, whose population is largely engaged in agriculture, I feel it is my duty to speak in this urgency debate on the agricultural situation.
In so doing, I am moved by a twofold feeling, Mr. Speaker. To begin with, I am rather pleased to take the floor because the farmers, in my region as in the rest of Canada, deserve that we give them our attention. But, at the same time, I am filled with grief when I see the extremely difficult situation which these people have been facing for a long time.
There is much talk in this house of the grain producers of the Prairie provinces and, undoubtedly, they are in a rather desperate situation this year.
However, the problem is not insurmountable for them, because some of them can take up cattle breeding and thus liberate that land used for grain-growing.
Mr. Speaker, such is not the case with the milk producers of the central provinces, particularly the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region, which I represent in this house, along with three colleagues.
In my constituency, most of the farmers are engaged in the dairy industry, because of the difficult weather conditions. Indeed, they have to switch to dairy production or give up farming altogether.
Over the past years, various farm authorities have advised them to expand their operations in order to increase their production and to modernize it in order to improve its quality. That is what they have done.
In my constituency, over the past ten years, their number has decreased by half, so that today they number only about 2,300, with an annual production of about 235,000,000 pounds of milk, which represents approximately 100,000 pounds of milk per producer. They borrowed money to make improvements, and they badly need their income to hold out.
May 1. 1969

That is why, even though I recognize the difficulties which production surpluses cause the Department of Agriculture, I must protest on behalf of the 2,300 producers of my area and others in Canada, against the new policy announced by the Canadian Dairy Commission on March 31 last.
I protest all the more as this new policy seems to have been adopted without consultations with representatives of the producers concerned, as to other solutions which might have been applied in the circumstances.
I heard a moment ago the hon. member for Boberval (Mr. Gauthier) quote the brief submitted to us Monday by the representatives of agricultural associations in his area. 1 shall not quote parts of the same brief, but I must say that, in my opinion, most of the grievances expressed there are well-founded.
More than 400 dairy producers came to that meeting, Mr. Speaker, to support their leaders, and the least I can say is that they were not very happy. They said so very clearly.
Nobody questioned the fact that the price situation had greatly improved in the last years, especially since the establishment of the Canadian Dairy Commission, but the setback they will suffer this year because of the new policy seems unacceptable to them. For them and for farmers in my area, that represents a loss of about $280,000 this year, and that, in an area already suffering from an 18 per cent unemployment rate. That is not likely to solve our problem.
Mr. Speaker, if in the last two years some
39,000	farmers went out of business in the dairy industry, we could at least have tried to reduce the surplus production through some other policy than the present farm policy or migration from the farms by producers, which will certainly continue. Besides, we should ask ourselves whether every effort is being made in order to find markets for our milk surplus.
As I have only ten minutes left, Mr. Speaker, before concluding my remarks I would like to give an example of the disastrous effects of the new dairy policy. This applies not only to my district but to the province of Quebec and the country as a whole.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Four years ago, at Saint-Coeur-de-Marie, in the Lac-Saint-Jean area, a young man of 30 bought a 200-acre piece of land with money he had saved when working in the Chibouga-mau mines; he also acquired a herd. However, as he decided to increase it, the Canadian
Business of Supply
Dairy Commission came into existence. He was given a quota based on his first year of operation, that is a production of 100,000 pounds of milk. Now, with the new policy, after having increased his production to 300,000 pounds, this young man is placed in the position where he would have to pay the Dairy Commission $50 a year. He would thus not make any profit and would even have to pay in order to operate his business. This is inconceivable. I therefore wonder how it will be possible to solve the problem of milk surplus.
The answer is not easy to find, of course, and it is impossible to find a quick solution to this problem while trying to stay within reasonable costs. We are told that in 1969 the Canadian taxpayer will pay around $125 million in subsidies to that industry and that the population as a whole, will pay another $100 million, because prices will be higher, since there is an embargo on imports.
I suggest that, on a trial basis, a committee be appointed which would be made up of representatives of producers as well as representatives of the department, who would have the necessary powers to negotiate a reasonable agreement, at least temporarily, with a view to settling this problem. If the producers were a party to this agreement, they would probably be more ready to cooperate in the implementation of these directives. For a while, it would probably cost a few millions more, but one could hope, at least, for a final settlement of the problem. Perhaps subsidies could be further reduced, even eliminated; that would be ideal, of course, and the net income of the producer would not be reduced as much.
I strongly urge the minister to seriously consider the setting up of that mechanism of negotiation, at least as an experience, because it is imperative to find a solution to this problem.
I cannot close without commenting on the recent changes in the method of classification of hogs in my area. Under the previous system, 40 to 60 per cent of hogs were getting a premium, but since the new standards went into effect at the beginning of the year, this rate has declined to 35 per cent.
However, recognizing the value of the new system, producers have accepted it without too much opposition, hoping to adapt themselves to it rather quickly, that is over a period of 12 to 18 months. But hardly four months later, these requirements were changed, which resulted in getting premiums

May 1, 1969
Business of Supply
for only 18 per cent of the hogs at the slaughter-house.
Even if the price has substantially increased on the market, as everyone agrees, the fact remains that, because of the disastrous situation during the three preceding years, producers need this surplus to make up for accumulated deficits.
The least that could have been done would have been to wait a few more months in order to allow the producers to get used to this new system.
As I often get the chance to speak with the minister, I shall continue to use my influence with him, because, as I know him particularly well, I am aware of his great ability in the field of agriculture and of his very great concern for the human problem which the present agricultural situation implies. I believe that the human problem is primarily the one with which we should be dealing.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate initiated by the official opposition, and pleased that the debate has taken place because of the minister's apparent lack of understanding of the exact conditions in western Canada. Of course, I mean the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), although having listened to the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) this statement could also apply to him.

I wish to quote briefly from the brief presented by the Premier of Saskatchewan, a Liberal premier, to the Standing Committee on Agriculture during the course of its tour of the western provinces. The Minister of Agriculture, who has been a Liberal for only a short time, may learn something from this brief. In it the premier said:
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of the government of Saskatchewan may I say that in our opinion the western grain industry faces a major crisis.
Could anyone make that more clear? Today, I listened to the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture. He dealt with the

subject of livestock, and said how great that industry is. Good as it is, it is thanks to no help from him, and thank heaven for that. Surely, because the livestock industry is in good shape, this does not necessarily mean the whole economy is in good shape.
I see the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) on the edge of his seat as if he had something knowledgeable to say.

The economic circumstances of a majority of prairie producers are desperate.
So, beyond a shadow of a doubt we have a major crisis in western agriculture.

Until then he had dealt with apples, potatoes, the livestock industry, the hog industry, chickens and eggs. He skated around the main problem. I didn't even know he was a hockey player. Mr. Speaker, I am not pleased to take part in this debate because it should not be necessary. I was not pleased to see some 20,000 people turn out at 24 different meetings in Saskatchewan. I was not pleased to see between
6,000	and 8,000 at the S.F.U. meeting at Saskatoon protesting the way this government is handling the feed grain situation. I think this would all be unnecessary if the government would face up to the situation.
I say that the position taken today by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) certainly was that of a very benevolent individual bleeding for the agricultural economy. This is the first impression and one that sets the stage for the great defeat of the agricultural economy. It is a double-cross from the word go.
Let us take a look at the record which indicates the reason given by an irresponsible government for not really meeting the crisis

May 1. 1969
Business of Supply
head on. We have only to look at what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had to say yesterday. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) quoted the Prime Minister as saying yesterday that the economy is on the move and things never have been so good. I am sure the people in western Canada will remember this Statement for years to come. I am sure that the Liberal candidates in the next election will have to justify this statement many times.
Today, the Minister of Agriculture spoke like a great white father. He told us the farmers never had it so good so far as cash advances were concerned. If I understood him correctly, I believe he said 83,000 farmers have taken advantage of cash advances compared to 45,000 last year. These simple facts prove there is a serious crisis facing our primary producers which the government is not prepared, or does not want, to meet. I ask the minister and the government to do something now rather than gloat over what they have done in the immediate past.
The minister spent some time quoting glowing figures. He mentioned prices in respect of other products. If he would look at the facts, he would realize that good steers today should sell at $35.99 per hundredweight; that grade A hogs should sell at $53.85 per hundredweight; that wheat should sell at $3.27 per bushel and that shelled corn should sell at $2.10 per bushel. I ask whether the minister really has uttered any great, magic words of condolence to the people who are not receiving these amounts of money. I am sure the producers would feel a little more confident if they knew they could turn to other products, such as those referred to by the minister, but they would have no guarantee so far as prices of those products are concerned. The suggestion that the farmer should turn to these products at this time means absolutely nothing to him because he has no idea what he would receive on his investment at a future date. It is hypocritical for the minister to bring in such a suggestion.
I should like to move briefly to the subject of feed grain. I am sure the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon (Mr. Lang) is well aware of this subject. If he is not, he should be. In Saskatoon, when some 6,000 to 8,000 farmers gathered to protest the movement of feed grain between provinces, this minister stood up and tried to talk like a professor to practical people. This did not work and no one knows it better than the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon.
[Mr. Skoberg.l
This government, and particularly the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and even the Attorney General, stand accused in the eyes of the people of the west for doing absolutely nothing when they knew this smuggling was taking place. When these people gathered at Saskatoon on April 11, they produced documentary evidence that feed grain was being smuggled. This is going on constantly. We know that some 5,000 bushels per day of feed grain are going from Saskatchewan to Alberta at a price of between 40 cents and 60 cents a bushel. We know the Canadian Wheat Board is aware of this. We know there must be a directive from somebody in the government telling these people to turn their eyes away and do nothing about it.
I, personally, have phoned the department to ask what could be done about it. All that happens is that one is shoved from department to department; they have no intention of doing anything. Many people in the west are asking why something is not being done about the movement of feed grain. The people in the west are familiar with the fact that the ranchers, food processing plants and packers like to have this type of movement continue. This makes one wonder whether or not there is some collusion between these people and others to make sure that nothing will be done about it. As late as the 25th of this month, the following advertisement appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix:
Required immediately 1,000,000 bu. No. 2 hard wheat. Will pay 70c cash per bushel delivered to nearest elevator.
Then, a box number is given.
I ask the minister whether he intends to sit there doing nothing while this type of procedure is being conducted. We do not know what elevator is being used to obtain this grain without permit books. If permit books are being used, it is illegal. I think it is only right that this government should stand on its own feet and do something for those people who are drawing this situation to their attention. I wonder how we could possibly say we support the Canadian Wheat Board when it has not really been given the authority to market the grain it should market. What the people in the west really want is that the Wheat Board be given the authority to market grain in an orderly fashion. The farmers want a fair return on their investment. I can assure you that under present circumstances in the west there is no opportunity to receive a fair return on any type of investment. I
May 1, 1969



most heartily support the suggestion put forward by my colleague that an income sufficiency payment is needed now, not tomorrow.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The immediate need is for the payment of 20 cents per bushel of grain on a maximum of
5,000	bushels. At one of the meetings in Moose Jaw I believe one of the farmers put it very aptly. He said: "We have waited in vain with patience and too long now for promised programs that would provide some solutions to our problems". I should like to quote an article written by George Bain, which appeared in the Globe and Mail of March 11, 1969. It is headed, "A protest from the West", and reads as follows:
Read Bruce Hutchison in Saturday's Globe and Mail: "...The people of the west are beginning to suspect that they have in Ottawa not a genuine national government but an Ontario-Quebec government too concentrated in the Laurentian centre, too French, and too careless of the perimeter, both Western and Atlantic".
I am sure those people in the other areas of Canada can subscribe to the idea that the west and the far east are not getting their fair share or a return on their investment. I am sure that the people will not stand by and accept much longer that which is being forced on them.
Before I conclude, may I put a question which I believe the government should answer: Does the federal Liberal party support the orderly marketing of feed grains under the quotas and pricing system of the Canadian Wheat Board? The Minister without Portfolio did not answer that question in Saskatoon when it was put to him. I believe it is an obligation of this government to tell the people of this nation whether or not they support the Canadian Wheat Board and whether or not they support the orderly marketing of grains. Nothing else will do at this time.
I am sure that all of us here are sincere when we ask the government to take immediate action to supply cash for the benefit of the western agricultural economy. I am sure that everyone here is sincere when they say it can be done and it must be done. If the government does not act now, they will forever know that they deliberately destroyed the entire agricultural economy of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to inform the house of my views on what I have heard since noon,
Business of Supply
of what I think of the motion of non-confidence blaming the government for its administration especially with regard to agricultural matters.
I was surprised to hear all those who supported this motion, especially the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who surprised me all the more as he was the only one who did not propose any solution to the problem. That surprised me greatly.
I recall certain facts which may help me to explain later on why my feeling of surprise disappeared fairly quickly. I do it with much conviction, Mr. Speaker, because the lot of those who till the land in order to provide food for their fellowmen has never been easy except in times of famine or war, and it has been so in every country in the world. We must acknowledge that.
When efforts are made during difficult periods to improve the situation of agriculture, perhaps something else than what was done this afternoon should be tried. Instead of blaming, we must find solutions.
Was the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Dan-forth) who proposed the motion truly sincere? We shall analyse that problem together and thus we shall be able to decide whether or not we should support the motion. As for me, I feel that I do not even have the right to back it, but let us analyse the problem.
If my information is correct, the hon. member introduced this motion as a result of the policy of the present government to improve the dairy industry. Because time is limited, I shall try to limit myself to the dairy industry.
So, I told myself: Things are not too bad even now, for when the party of the hon. member was in power-there were then 208 members in the government-there was no policy, and I myself was a farmer at that time.
If one should decide to find out how serious the suggestions are that were made, including those of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), one could consult available figures and discover that in 1962-at which time the conservatives were in power-they were not led by the present Leader of the Opposition, who doubtless heard the unpleasant news- the Canadian dairy production was worth only $13,257,869. We see a change from 1963 to 1969: the dairy industry alone has now reached a production of $136,000,000.
A look at the total budget for 1961-62 reveals that $240,581,231 were allotted to agriculture. In the budget for 1969-70, over

May 1. 1969
Business of Supply
$280,000,000 are earmarked for agriculture alone.
In 1958, I was having problems on the farm, just as everyone else did in every sector of society in Eastern Canada, because support prices had gone down; that happened under the Progressive Conservatives regime.
I am hardly in a position to discuss the problems the West had to face in those days for I was not involved at that time as I am today. As for those of the East, I have experienced them myself. In fact, the price of bacon had gone down to the point that in 1958 and 1959 I was selling it at $17.80 per hundred pounds. That was not under the present administration.
If I mention this, it is in order to assess the arguments put forward today. If they are genuine, let us put the blame on those who were in charge of the country at that time, the same who are unable today to offer any answer to the increase in production costs.
I am certainly not too happy over that myself but those who can do no better than put the blame on others are not, in my opinion, very fair. And those who say that the government did not take the necessary steps are simply changing the terms of the problem. But when you say it has taken no efficient steps and is unable to take any, I think you are entirely wrong.
Mr. Speaker, when we were discussing the milk quotas, a member of the N.D.P. said that the Canadian Dairy Commission had penalized the farmers when fixing their milk quotas. Here again, in all fairness, all hon. members, to whatever political party they belong, should admit that many farmers are doing a job for which they are not fit, on land, in eastern Canada, which does not suit the dairy industry.
If you want to help us, get the money elsewhere, from the Welfare Department or the Unemployment Insurance Commission, but do not try to grant subsidies so as to induce the people to believe we are crying on their shoulders because the dairy industry will be facing the same problem ten years from now on.
Then, let us agree to impose quotas even if we run the risk of losing votes and even if the farm associations run the risk of losing contributions. But the first step is necessary. Now, the Canadian Dairy Commission has almost taken this step but it hurts to see young people finding it hard to follow suit. The farm associations, together with the Canadian Dairy Commission have asked that [Mr. Cote (Richelieu) .1
one should not let any more people engage in dairy production in order to help those who are now engaging in it.
Let us not forget that we have already imported butter from New Zealand. What was the policy before such imports were allowed? Today it is probably economic to import some but only as a guarantee and not for consumption. We must be assured not to run short. The Commission has two roles to play. It must promote the marketing of dairy products and protect the consumers to prevent the price of butter from becoming exorbitant.
Last year, 3.3 million pounds of butter were imported from New Zealand though we did not need it. It did not cost anything; it was simply resold. We did it in order to protect ourselves remembering what happened in 1962. The members of the opposition must remember, because there was no dairy policy concerning butter and we had to store in the government warehouses over 260 million pounds of butter in 1962. It cost the Treasury of our country over $60 million to get rid of this butter to resell it in any form, since we were forced to melt some of it.
The money was taken out of the pocket of the taxpayers, and we did not complain. The opposition did not complain either, despite the fact that there was no policy.
Today the situation is more stable. Because some butter is imported for protection, they complain and they cry shame.
Since this afternoon no hon. member has proposed any real solution. As for the quotas, as I said a while ago, we will all have to accept the government policy, whatever party we belong to.
This will hurt a few. Even for the small farmer who does not produce enough to make a living, we will have to implement policies like the present one. We cannot tell him that we should have helped him, because then that would be cutting our own necks. We should rather say, altogether: We know that we have to stop producing, and that it will hurt. We know that we will lose votes, in one party as well as in the other.
But if we really want to solve the problems of the dairy industry, we will have to fall into step.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I should like to begin by saying that I have had the pleasure of talking to a number of those who served on the standing committee as well as with Wheat Pool committee men. I am sure the Wheat Pool in Saskatchewan is to be commended on the wonderful job it did in organizing its business throughout the province of Saskatchewan. Above all, the members of the various pool committees are to be commended on the excellent briefs they presented to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I am sure it would be a good exercise for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to read these briefs, if he has not already done so. I am sure he would not continue to hold the view that there is no problem facing western agriculture. I also believe it would be well for him to read the brief submitted to the Committee by the Liberal premier of Saskatchewan. He would then agree, I feel, that there are problems facing agriculture, not only in western Canada, but right across the country.
It is significant that it should have been left to the opposition to bring before parliament a question of basic social and economic concern, one which should have been assigned top priority by any government with a serious desire to tackle the real problems confronting this nation. In my view, one of the most serious weaknesses of the present administration is its failure to face up to the urgent problems weighing upon ordinary people in this country. As a member for a riding that is largely rural, and a rural western riding at that, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the problems facing the industry of agriculture because I have become increasingly aware over the past months of the growing gulf between that industry and this government.
When one considers the tremendous importance of agriculture to the Canadian economy as a whole, when one realizes the number of Canadians intimately affected by the state of agriculture and when one recognizes the full social and economic implications of a sick
Business of Supply
agricultural industry for our standard of living and development as a nation, it is remarkable that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his colleagues should have allowed this gulf to occur and to widen. It is even more remarkable that no attempt has been made to bridge this gulf.
The evidence clearly indicates that the policy-makers of the Liberal party have weighed Canadian agriculture in political terms and have declared it expendable. I will not labour the evidence supplied by the present depressed state of the grain industry. This is already well known and the shameful record is clear for all to see-tons of dry, marketable wheat piled on farms across the prairies side by side with mountains of damp, unsaleable grain.
This government has failed all along the line. What measures were taken fall into the category of too little and too late. Inadequate assistance to farmers to meet the natural disaster of damp grain; chaos in the reception arrangements and shipment to the ports, bumbling in untying the railway transportation knot; too little of the right grain and too much of the wrong grain in terminal elevators; lost sales and failure to make significant new sales abroad. If it were not for the prior commitments to purchase made by Russia and China several years ago, the Canadian grain industry would today be bankrupt and in ruin.
Not once during its brief lifetime has this government brought forward one major piece of agricultural legislation. This house has seen a series of minor bills dealing with various aspects of agriculture, but the majority have been merely amendments to take the ceiling off various interest rates.
Not once has a senior minister mentioned the possibility of this government bringing forward a major measure dealing with basic agricultural policy. All we have seen has been a callous disregard for the very real problems of the industry and the depressed economic conditions now being experienced by those engaged in agriculture. This government has been responsible for parliament frittering away its time on minor matters such as the amendment to the Criminal Code.
The Canadian farmer is not interested in legally being able to engage in homosexual practices. What he wants is some assurance that he will be able to maintain a decent standard of living. The farmer with a glut of unsaleable grain on his hands, no credit at the bank and bills piling up disastrously, is

May 1. 1969
Business of Supply
not too concerned with legalized abortion or changes in the rules governing firearms.
Throughout the agricultural community today many thousands of solid, hard-working Canadians are beset by the devils of a real economic depression. They have every right to expect their government at least to recognize their plight. It is now obvious from the legislative plans of this government that there is no room for them in the "Just Society". They have been ignored by Ottawa, excluded from government policy and planning and sacrificed to other interests and other areas, and I speak of agriculture in all parts of Canada, not just in the west. It is almost as if the Prime Minister and his government were actively antagonistic to agriculture.
What little attention has been paid by the Minister of Agriculture to the farmers of Canada has been negative: "Don't do this, don't do that, don't grow wheat, grow something else, don't expect the government to sell your products."
There is much to be said for the suggestion of a two-price system for grain, but so far it is just another suggestion, a hint of something the minister may some day, just possibly, get around to discussing with his colleagues. What the Canadian farmer needs right now is reassurance that he is not forgotten, that he has not been written off. He wants to know that he can continue to enjoy the same standard of living as his fellow citizen in industrial Canada and that he will share equally in national prosperity, national development and national life.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The Canadian farmer needs some assistance from government. He needs this assistance to meet the uncertainties nature imposes, to meet stronger foreign competition and the radically changed market place for agricultural produce. He needs the same kind of degree of government assistance as any other segment of the economy.
The farmer needs guidance from government. If government is to make suggestions that mean a basic change in his mode of work and life, if government largely controls the purchase and marketing of his produce, then he needs government guidance to ensure his future. Above all, he needs government leadership; leadership that will reassure, uplift and inspire him. So far, this government has failed to supply any of these things.
I could get specific, Mr. Speaker, and go into detail about the deplorable state of dairy

farming, for instance. I could give you chapter and verse with regard to cases of young, able and willing farmers who cannot start in the dairy business, the business of their choice, because of government policies that create injustice, inequality and impose an economic burden no young Canadian can shoulder.
I believe that this house today should be most concerned with the general question of agriculture as well as this government's abject failure to provide answers to its many serious problems. I believe this house should be even more concerned with this government's obvious determination to ignore the agricultural community.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, having recently visited western Canada I find it shameful that so many farmers are at a loss about putting in a crop this spring.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from an agricultural area as I do, and also having visited the west with the agricultural committee, I feel that during the next few minutes I should like to say something about this important subject. If I may get right down to the nuts and bolts of the situation, the problem is just this: As many speakers have said, we have an over abundance of wheat and other foodstuffs in this country. The solution to the problem is to get out into the markets of the world and try to sell this foodstuff.
I am not suggesting that a great deal has not been done in this connection in the past. I went out west as a greenhorn as far as western agriculture was concerned-perhaps I came back the same way-but I did learn certain things about the Wheat Board that I did not know before. I should like to go on record right now as saying I agree with the general feeling in western Canada that when the Wheat Board was created some years ago it did a most remarkable job in stabilizing the wheat situation, which was in chaos.
However, I suggest to the house tonight that as a sales agency the Canadian Wheat Board has not been as successful as perhaps it should have been. In the last few years, Canada sold wheat and grain to 118 countries. That figure is in the Wheat Board's report. Yet last year we called on only 36 countries. Is this the way to do business? Is this the way other companies that sell coal, baking powder or Red Rose tea do business? We have to get out and see people before we can
May 1. 1969

sell them goods. If we are going to sell wheat to China, we will have to send to China people who are prepared to use chopsticks, drink Chinese wine and eat their rice. We must associate with them and become jolly good fellows so that, like private enterprise, we are able to sell our products.
In this regard, we have a fantastic advantage over our United States friends because we sell to communist countries. The United States sells very little to communist countries. As a matter of fact, the Chinese would sooner starve to death than buy United States wheat, so automatically they come to Canada. Last year we sold 133 million bushels of wheat to communist countries.
As all hon. members know, there is presently a world glut of wheat. Although Canadian officials tell me we cannot sell wheat, last year the United States increased its sales to foreign countries from 742 million bushels to 753 million bushels?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Because they went out and sold it. They went to work. You cannot expect the little farmers of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba to go out and sell wheat to Russia, Cuba, Hungary, France or whoever it may be. You have to have a sales organization to do that for you. It is the obligation of the government to set up this sales organization and to send it out to sell wheat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I regard as a downright shame the fact that last year we sold only 27 per cent as much wheat as the United States sold to the so-called free world. There seems to me something wrong with the way we are doing business. We have to go out and say hello to these people.
How does the Ford Motor Company, General Motors or any private enterprise business sell their products? What would Ford or General Motors do if they had too many cars? They would go out and sell them. This is what we have to do with our wheat.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE CAPITAL TO AGRICULTURE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in this discussion on the non-confidence motion against the government.
We would not want to blame the government overmuch, but we have to upbraid them, because we are still looking for an adequate agricultural policy. The government, with a good Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), have not yet found a solution to the serious agricultural problems.
Mr. Speaker, I am going to fight for the farmers of the Eastern Townships, because I am from that area and the farmers I represent are mainly engaged in dairy production.
Mr. Speaker, we have wanted reforms for a long time; we are trying to straighten out all sort of conditions, but the nostrums used up to now were of no avail. The Eastern Townships' farmers are in a serious plight; never in the history of this country have we seen them in such parlous circumstances.
A while ago, I heard the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cote) say that this government

Division

However, I would like to remind him that all the government has done bore no fruit; it did not solve anything, and there will soon be no farmers left in the Eastern Townships and in the province of Quebec. Indeed, farmers are on the verge of bankruptcy. Never was agriculture so near bankruptcy as it is today.
Mr. Speaker, since I have only a few minutes at my disposal, I should like to deal with the element missing to solve the problem. Farmers pay too much tax on building materials. They are overtaxed. Their machines cost too much.
Since agriculture is a basic industry in our country, interest rates should be brought down, because the farmers should not always be the ones who have to make sacrifices. The hon. member for Richelieu said earlier that if farmers are not able to pay a 10 per cent interest rate, they should quit. I think the hon. member for Richelieu is standing up for finance.
